children.name: Sepsis Prediction
children.blurb: Sepsis prediction in intensive care and hospital wards uses machine learning to estimate the risk of sepsis onset or deterioration before clinical recognition.

children.name: Acute Kidney Injury Prediction
children.blurb: Acute kidney injury prediction uses routinely collected clinical data to estimate a patient's risk of developing AKI during a hospital stay, often in intensive care.

children.name: Ventilator Weaning
children.blurb: Ventilator weaning models aim to predict when a mechanically ventilated patient can safely breathe without the machine.

children.name: Fall Risk Monitoring
children.blurb: Fall risk monitoring in predictive patient analytics and intensive care estimates the probability that a patient will fall during a hospital stay, with particular attention to intensive care step-down and post-surgical units where mobility changes quickly.

children.name: Staffing and Bed Forecasting
children.blurb: Staffing and bed forecasting uses predictive models to estimate patient admissions, discharges, transfers, and acuity in intensive care and general wards.

sections.body: Predictive patient analytics in intensive care uses machine learning on electronic health records, vital signs, lab results, and nursing notes to estimate risks that may develop hours or days later. In current practice, models flag possible sepsis before a clinician sees the full pattern, calculate the chance of acute kidney injury after contrast or surgery, suggest when a ventilated patient might tolerate a breathing trial, watch movement and room sensors for fall risk, and project how many beds and nurses a unit will need. These tools produce scores, alerts, or forecasts that a human team reviews. They do not make treatment decisions on their own. The work is decision support, not automation of care.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field has many published models but fewer that are trusted in a live intensive care unit. This site tracks 1000 medical AI models, 803 of them scientific models, and the gap between those two numbers reflects how much work remains before these tools are dependable at the bedside. Sepsis alerts still generate many false alarms, kidney injury models can miss unusual cases, ventilator weaning suggestions may be too cautious or too aggressive, fall monitoring depends on sensor coverage, and staffing forecasts break down during sudden surges. Legal accountability is also unsettled, with six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies tracked here. No model replaces clinical judgment, and none of these predictions should be treated as certain.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Sepsis Prediction is the most studied ICU alert, covering early warning scores, model types, and the tradeoff between catching cases and flooding staff with alarms. Acute Kidney Injury Prediction focuses on creatinine trends and medication exposure, showing where models help and where they fail. Ventilator Weaning addresses the timing of breathing trials and extubation, a decision where false confidence is dangerous. Fall Risk Monitoring moves from physiology to movement and environment, using sensors and video rather than lab values. Staffing and Bed Forecasting is the operational layer, turning individual risk estimates into unit level demand for nurses and beds. Together these pages move from single patient deterioration to ward capacity.
